"Police on the scene quickly determined that Walkinshaw had been the driver of the vehicle. While paramedics tended to the injured young woman, who was later airlifted to Royal Darwin Hospital in a stable condition, officers placed Walkinshaw under arrest for driving under the influence and a series of related offences.

According to the coronial inquest, Walkinshaw was visibly distressed at the scene. He was crying, apologising repeatedly, and expressing concern for the woman he had been with. One of the arresting officers later told the inquest that Walkinshaw appeared "shaken but cooperative," and that there was no immediate indication he posed a risk to himself.

Walkinshaw was placed in the rear caged compartment of the police vehicle for transport to the Darwin watch house. The journey, according to police records, took approximately 22 minutes. During that time, neither officer in the front of the vehicle conducted a visual check on their passenger.

When the vehicle arrived at the watch house and the rear cage was opened, Walkinshaw was found unresponsive. He had used an item of his own clothing to take his own life. Despite immediate attempts at resuscitation by officers and paramedics, he was pronounced dead a short time later.

Cavanagh's findings, handed down this week, were scathing of the Northern Territory Police Force's failure to implement recommendations made years earlier. In 2013, following the death of another man in similar circumstances, an internal review had recommended that CCTV cameras be installed in all caged police vehicles to allow officers to monitor detainees during transport. That recommendation, the coroner noted, had been "essentially ignored" for three years.

"The evidence before this inquest paints a deeply troubling picture," Cavanagh wrote. "Sixteen attempted suicides in the back of caged vehicles over a three-year period, six of which were only discovered when the person was already semi-conscious or unconscious. These are not isolated incidents. They represent a systemic failure."

The coroner heard evidence from a senior officer who acknowledged that budgetary constraints had been cited as a reason for not installing the cameras, though Cavanagh dismissed this explanation as "wholly inadequate" given the demonstrated risk to life.

Walkinshaw's family, who attended much of the inquest, described him as a young man who had struggled with mental health issues and substance abuse but who had been making efforts to turn his life around. His mother told the inquest that her son had recently begun seeing a counsellor and had spoken about returning to study.

"Dale wasn't a bad person," she said in a statement read to the court. "He made a terrible mistake that night, and he knew it. He needed help, not to be left alone in the back of a van."

Cavanagh made a series of recommendations, including the immediate installation of CCTV cameras in all NT Police caged vehicles, mandatory welfare checks at intervals no greater than ten minutes during transport, and improved mental health screening protocols at the point of arrest.

The Northern Territory Police Commissioner issued a statement acknowledging the coroner's findings and committing to implementing the recommendations "as a matter of urgency." Installation of CCTV equipment in caged vehicles has reportedly begun across the territory.

For Walkinshaw's family, however, the changes come too late. "We don't want another family to go through what we've been through," his mother said outside court. "If they had just listened in 2013, our boy might still be here.""
